The confidence intervals grow wider as the forecast horizon increases due to compounding uncertainties. In the short term (1 day), uncertainty is minimal because there is less time for external factors or random noise to introduce deviations. Over a 1-week horizon, more variables could come into play, such as market fluctuations, news events, or other unexpected changes, so the interval widens. By 1 month, even greater uncertainty arises, as the accumulation of small deviations, unforeseen events, or broader market trends could create larger swings in the outcomes. Additionally, variability in historical data or model assumptions contributes to the growing range of possible outcomes as time progresses.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated confidence intervals. In the shorter term, these might include sudden shocks, such as unexpected economic announcements, major geopolitical events, or natural disasters, which weren't factored into the baseline model. Over longer timeframes, other risks like policy changes, economic downturns, or an accumulation of smaller, unexpected deviations could push the actual value significantly beyond the upper or lower bounds of the forecast. These intervals assume normal conditions and trends—major disruptions or structural shifts could make them less reliable.
